# 5.1 Ridge regression {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## The estimator

$$\hat\beta^{\text{ridge}} = \arg\min_\beta \Big\{ \|y - X\beta\|_2^2 + \lambda\|\beta\|_2^2 \Big\}
= (X^\top X + \lambda I)^{-1} X^\top y$$

The added $\lambda I$ makes the matrix positive definite for **any** $\lambda > 0$, even when
$p > n$.

::: {.check}
Regularisation is not only a bias–variance device. It is what makes the problem **well-posed at
all**.
:::

## What ridge does, in the SVD basis

With $X = UDV^\top$:

$$\hat y^{\text{ridge}} = \sum_{j=1}^{p} u_j \frac{d_j^2}{d_j^2 + \lambda} \, u_j^\top y$$

Compare OLS — the same sum with **every factor equal to 1**.

## Targeted, not blunt

Ridge multiplies the $j$-th principal component of the design by
$d_j^2/(d_j^2+\lambda) \in (0,1)$.

::: {.tight}
- **Large** $d_j$ — where the data vary a lot — barely touched
- **Small** $d_j$ — where the data are nearly collinear and the OLS coefficient is wildly unstable — shrunk hard
:::

::: {.check}
A *targeted* damping of exactly the directions in which your data carry little information.
:::

## Effective degrees of freedom

$$\mathrm{df}(\lambda) = \sum_j \frac{d_j^2}{d_j^2+\lambda}$$

decreasing smoothly from $p$ to $0$.

::: {.muted}
The Session 04 quantity, made concrete. There is no "number of parameters" here — there is a dial.
:::

## Bias–variance, explicitly

$\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta^{\text{ridge}})$ is **decreasing** in $\lambda$ while
$\operatorname{Bias}^2$ is **increasing**.

> There always exists $\lambda > 0$ whose MSE is **strictly lower than OLS**.

::: {.check}
A result that surprised the profession in 1970, and it should still shape how you think about
Gauss–Markov. BLUE was never a promise about total error.
:::

# 5.2 The lasso {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## The estimator

$$\hat\beta^{\text{lasso}} = \arg\min_\beta \Big\{ \tfrac{1}{2n}\|y - X\beta\|_2^2 + \lambda\|\beta\|_1 \Big\}$$

No closed form.

::: {.muted}
Note the $\tfrac{1}{2n}$ scaling — it is what makes $\lambda$ comparable across sample sizes, and
it is the convention `glmnet` and scikit-learn use.
:::

## Why the corners matter

In the equivalent constrained form — minimise RSS subject to $\|\beta\|_1 \le t$ — the constraint
region is a **cross-polytope** (a diamond in 2-D), which has **corners on the axes**.

The elliptical RSS contours expanding outward from $\hat\beta^{OLS}$ meet this region, generically,
**at a corner** — and a corner is a point where some coordinates are exactly zero.

::: {.check}
The $\ell_2$ ball is smooth. It has no corners, so ridge shrinks but never zeroes. Sparsity is a
property of the *shape*.
:::

## Coordinate descent

Hold all $\beta_k$, $k\neq j$, fixed. With standardised columns
($\frac1n\sum_i x_{ij}^2 = 1$), the univariate problem is

$$\min_{\beta_j} \; \tfrac{1}{2}(\beta_j - \rho_j)^2 + \lambda|\beta_j|$$

$$\rho_j = \tfrac1n \textstyle\sum_i x_{ij}\big(y_i - \sum_{k\neq j} x_{ik}\beta_k\big)$$

::: {.muted}
$\rho_j$ is the partial correlation of $x_j$ with the current residual.
:::

## Soft-thresholding

The objective is convex but **non-differentiable at 0**. Using the subgradient of $|\beta_j|$ —
which is $[-1,1]$ at zero — the solution is

$$\hat\beta_j = S_\lambda(\rho_j) = \operatorname{sign}(\rho_j)\,\big(|\rho_j| - \lambda\big)_+$$

## Read it directly

> If the partial correlation of $x_j$ with the residual is smaller in magnitude than $\lambda$, set
> the coefficient to **exactly zero**; otherwise **shrink it toward zero by $\lambda$**.

::: {.check}
Cycling this update over $j$ converges — and it is why `glmnet` and scikit-learn are fast.
:::

::: {.warn}
Note the second clause. Surviving coefficients are still **biased toward zero**. The lasso selects
*and* shrinks, and people routinely forget the second part when reading magnitudes.
:::

## Limitations you must know

::: {.tight}
1. With $p > n$, the lasso selects **at most $n$** variables.
2. Among a group of highly correlated predictors it tends to pick **one arbitrarily** and zero the
   rest — unstable across samples, and often economically absurd.
3. Its selected set is consistent only under strong conditions (the **irrepresentable condition**).
:::

::: {.warn}
**Do not present a lasso path as if it identified the true model.**
:::

# 5.3 The elastic net {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## Both penalties

$$\hat\beta^{\text{EN}} = \arg\min_\beta \Big\{ \tfrac{1}{2n}\|y-X\beta\|_2^2
+ \lambda\big[\alpha \|\beta\|_1 + \tfrac{1-\alpha}{2}\|\beta\|_2^2\big] \Big\}, \qquad \alpha \in [0,1]$$

$\alpha = 1$ is the lasso; $\alpha = 0$ is ridge.

## The grouping effect

The mixed penalty is **strictly convex** whenever $\alpha < 1$. That delivers what Zou and Hastie
call the *grouping effect*:

::: {.tight}
- for two **identical** predictors, the elastic net assigns them **identical** coefficients — the lasso must choose
- more generally, the difference in coefficients is bounded by a function of
  $1 - \operatorname{corr}(x_j, x_k)$
:::

## Why this is not a technicality

For macroeconomic panels — where dozens of series measure nearly the same underlying construct —
this is the difference between a model that says

> *"industrial production matters"*

and one that says

> *"industrial production of durable goods excluding motor vehicles, specifically, and none of its
> neighbours."*

## The coordinate update

$$\hat\beta_j = \frac{S_{\lambda\alpha}(\rho_j)}{1 + \lambda(1-\alpha)}$$

::: {.muted}
Soft-threshold, then divide. One extra line of arithmetic over the lasso.
:::

# 5.4 Choosing the tuning parameters {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## The grid

Fit over a **decreasing** grid of $\lambda$ from

$$\lambda_{\max} = \frac{\max_j |x_j^\top y|}{n\alpha}$$

— the smallest $\lambda$ giving the null model — down to $\varepsilon\lambda_{\max}$, using **warm
starts**.

Cross-validate **jointly** over $(\alpha, \lambda)$.

## Two conventions

| | |
|---|---|
| $\lambda_{\min}$ | the value minimising CV error |
| $\lambda_{1\text{se}}$ | the **largest** $\lambda$ within one standard error of the minimum |

$\lambda_{1\text{se}}$ gives a simpler model whose performance is statistically indistinguishable.

::: {.check}
**Prefer it when the model must be explained to someone.** Which, in this course, it must.
:::

## Inference warning

::: {.warn}
Standard errors reported **after** lasso selection are **not valid**, because selection used the
same data. Naive post-selection $p$-values are badly anti-conservative.
:::

::: {.muted}
This is what motivates the debiased methods later in the course.
:::

# The lab {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## What you do

::: {.tight}
1. Build the design matrix on your angle; standardise **inside** the pipeline
2. Fit ridge, lasso and elastic net under **grouped** CV
3. Report the chosen $(\alpha, \lambda)$, and compare $\lambda_{\min}$ with $\lambda_{1\text{se}}$
4. Bootstrap the selection: how often does each predictor survive?
:::

::: {.check}
The **selection-frequency table** is the deliverable, not the coefficient table. Anyone can produce
the second.
:::

## The two-minute report

**One slide. Three sentences.**

::: {.tight}
1. **What I did** — the penalty, the CV scheme, the chosen parameters
2. **The number** — the selected set, with selection frequencies
3. **The catch** — that coefficients are shrunk, and that no p-value follows
:::

::: {.check}
Full brief: [`02-lab/README.md`](02-lab/README.md)
:::
